sections.heading: Methodology
paragraphs: The improved architecture this paper develops is a Fourier-enhanced, domain-decomposed Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN). It predicts electromagnetic interference (EMI) inside a printed circuit board (PCB), the layered board of copper and insulating material found in nearly every electronic device. The base architecture is a fully connected multilayer perceptron (MLP), the standard PINN backbone introduced by Raissi, Perdikaris, and Karniadakis [1]. The specific architecture this model enhances is the Extended Physics-Informed Neural Network (XPINN) [2], which splits the physical space into regions, each handled by its own network. This model builds on XPINN in two ways: adding per-subdomain Fourier feature embeddings inspired by Tancik et al. [3] and Wang and Perdikaris [4], and replacing XPINN's soft interface enforcement with a stronger mechanism at material boundaries.

A PINN suits this problem for three reasons. First, Maxwell's equations are the governing physics, and a PINN builds them directly into training as a penalty term, pushing the network toward physically consistent predictions even where no reference data exists. In first-order time-domain form these are:

where E and H are the electric and magnetic fields, ε and μ are the permittivity and permeability of the material, and σ_c is its conductivity. Second, the problem requires evaluating the field at any point rather than only fixed grid locations; a PINN stores the solution in its weights as a continuous function, so once trained it can be queried anywhere at almost no cost, unlike grid solvers that need interpolation or a finer re-run. Third, a PINN extends naturally to inverse problems, learning unknown material properties alongside the weights, which a grid solver cannot do without wrapping many forward simulations in an outer loop.

The predicted quantity is the full time-domain electromagnetic field: the three electric and three magnetic field components (Ex, Ey, Ez, Hx, Hy, Hz) as continuous functions of position and time. Stating this matters because "predicting EMI" can mean several things; some models predict frequency spectra, coupling between wire pairs, or radiated emissions. This project predicts the underlying field traveling through the copper traces and insulating layers of the PCB, from which those other quantities can be derived. The frequency range of interest is 1 to 10 GHz, covering modern high-speed digital connections. FR-4, the standard board insulator, has properties that vary slightly with frequency across this range; the current model treats them as fixed, a simplification a later model could remove.

The decomposition follows the full three-dimensional material geometry, not only the vertical layer stack. A vertical-only split gives one network per layer but misses key physics, since the copper traces (the thin copper wires patterned onto the board) sit within a layer, and the strongest interference comes from in-plane structure such as coupling between neighboring traces and behavior at trace edges. Subdomain boundaries are therefore placed at every material transition, including the lateral edges of traces.
The conditions at a boundary depend on its type. Between two insulators with no surface current, the fields are continuous across it, meaning the values on each side match:
n × (E₁ − E₂) = 0          n × (H₁ − H₂) = 0

At the surface of a conductor such as copper, the conditions differ. Copper conducts well, so the field inside effectively vanishes and it is standard to treat it as a perfect electric conductor. The tangential electric field is then zero at the surface, and the tangential magnetic field is discontinuous, with the jump equal to the surface current Js:
n × E = 0          n × (H₁ − H₂) = Js

Forcing the magnetic field to be continuous at a copper surface would tell the network there is no surface current, when those currents are the main source of the radiation being predicted. Copper regions are therefore treated as perfect-conductor boundaries rather than given their own networks, which also removes the instability caused by placing a very large conductivity value into the equations.

Enforcing the interface conditions requires a mechanism, since two separate networks cannot agree exactly at a shared boundary unless the architecture forces them to. Three options exist: a heavily weighted penalty in the loss, which stays soft no matter how large the weight; an output transformation, where the raw output passes through a fixed layer built so the condition holds automatically; or parameter sharing, where both networks read the boundary value from one shared output. This project uses an output transformation for the perfect-conductor condition, multiplying the tangential electric field by a function that vanishes at the surface so n × E = 0 holds by construction. The insulator-to-insulator conditions currently use a strongly weighted penalty, which is soft; moving these to a shared parameterization is the main remaining design task, and results are reported with this limitation noted. The first-order form of Maxwell's equations is used because Nohra and Dufour [5] found it converges better on interface problems than the second-order form.

The closest prior work, Nohra and Dufour [5, 6], also uses domain decomposition, but deliberately smooths over material discontinuities to avoid enforcing interface conditions. This project does the opposite, keeping boundaries sharp and enforcing conditions directly. Their approach trains more easily but loses accuracy in a thin band around each interface, while this one accepts harder training to keep that band accurate, since that region is where the interference originates. The two are opposite choices on the same problem, making theirs a direct comparison point.

Standard networks suffer from spectral bias, learning smooth low-frequency patterns far faster than sharp high-frequency ones, a problem when the field oscillates quickly in space. Tancik et al. [3] showed that passing inputs through sine and cosine functions before the network corrects this. The embedding maps an input coordinate vector v as:
γ(v) = [sin(2πBv), cos(2πBv)]

where B is a fixed frequency matrix whose rows are drawn from a Gaussian with standard deviation σ_B. Using different frequency scales for different parts of a problem is not new; Wang and Perdikaris [4] introduced multi-scale Fourier embeddings, which motivate this approach. What is specific here is tying each region's scale to the wavelength in that region's material:
λ = c / (f · √(εr μr))

so a denser material, where the field oscillates faster, gets a higher-frequency embedding. Combining this scale-matching with spatial decomposition is the contribution: Wang and Perdikaris did the multi-scale part without decomposition, and XPINN did decomposition without scale-matching.

This embedding is also the main feature engineering step. Instead of feeding raw coordinates to the network, each is expanded into a higher-dimensional set of sinusoidal features (128 per subdomain, from 64 frequency rows), which lets the network represent high-frequency field behavior. All six field components are predicted jointly; none are dropped and no dimensionality reduction is applied. The subdomain index acts as light feature selection, since each network sees only points within its own material region.

Because the residual is small across most of the domain and concentrated near boundaries and sources, uniform sampling wastes effort. Residual-based adaptive refinement, proposed by Lu et al. [8], periodically scores a pool of candidate points by error and adds the worst; that work is credited here for the sampling method, not only the software library. Wu et al. [9] improved this with RAR-D, which samples points in proportion to their error rather than taking the strict worst, and which performs better, so RAR-D is used. Sampling runs independently within each subdomain to work with the per-region embeddings.

No public dataset exists for this problem, so reference data is generated by finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulation, a standard grid-based method for solving Maxwell's equations. Ground-truth fields inside a 3D structure cannot be measured directly at fine resolution, so simulation is the accepted source of reference data. The solver is MEEP [7], an open-source FDTD package from MIT. The more common choice for board work is openEMS, so the reason for MEEP is practical: its native Python interface lets reference generation, sampling, and training run in one language with no conversion step, which matters when the solver is called repeatedly across geometries. MEEP also supports frequency-dependent materials, useful for the FR-4 extension noted above. Cross-checking against openEMS is future work.

For each geometry the reference data is the six field components sampled on a grid over a sequence of time steps. For the baseline three-layer PCB stackup (a copper-insulator-copper sandwich, the simplest form of a real board), the grid is roughly 64 × 64 × 38 points across 21 time steps, about 3.2 million points and 19 million field values. Units are non-dimensionalized, a standard rescaling that sets the physical constants to one and keeps values in a stable range. Exploratory analysis guided several choices: field magnitude spans about three orders of magnitude, so inputs are normalized and loss terms weighted separately; early-training error clusters near interfaces and the source, justifying adaptive sampling; and the field is near zero inside copper, supporting the perfect-conductor treatment.

Coordinates are normalized to [−1, 1] within each subdomain before the embedding, keeping the activation functions responsive; field values are used in normalized units. There are no missing values, images, or text to process, since the data comes from a deterministic solver on a complete grid, and no class imbalance to correct, since this is continuous regression rather than classification.

The usual train-validation-test split does not apply cleanly, since most of the training signal comes from the physics penalty at unlabeled points. The split that exists is between the small set of reference points used in the loss and the rest held out: 2,000 points (under 0.1% of the grid) are drawn at random for the data term, and the full remaining grid is used only for final evaluation. Collocation points, where the physics penalty is checked, are sampled separately from the geometry: 8,192 per subdomain, plus smaller sets on the boundaries, initial time, and interfaces. K-fold cross-validation does not apply, since generalization here means covering a continuous domain rather than generalizing across separate samples.

Training runs on a CUDA-capable GPU with automatic fallback to CPU. It is memory-intensive because the physics penalty requires differentiating through the networks, so reducing points per subdomain is the first step when memory is short, and candidate scoring is already chunked for this reason. MEEP installs through conda rather than pip and is awkward on Windows, so reference data is generated on Linux. PINN training can be unstable when penalty terms compete, handled with a two-phase schedule, Adam first for broad progress and L-BFGS second for fine convergence, plus fixed weights prioritizing the boundary and interface terms.
Accuracy is measured against the held-out FDTD reference. The primary metric is relative L2 error per field component, the size of the error over the size of the true field:
relative L2 error = ǁu_pred − u_trueǁ / ǁu_trueǁ

This is standard, keeping results comparable to published work. Others are reported because relative L2 alone hides specific failures: mean squared error, for comparison with papers that use it; normalized root mean squared error, an easily read percentage; maximum absolute error, since a model can be accurate on average but badly wrong in a small important region; relative L2 error measured only near interfaces, directly testing the central claim; the physics residual on held-out points, checking whether the network satisfies Maxwell's equations where it never trained rather than memorizing data; and inference time per query against FDTD run time, measuring the practical speedup.

The baseline is a standard PINN with no embedding, no decomposition, and uniform sampling, trained on the same geometry with the same size and budget. It is expected to perform poorly, and confirming it fails in the predicted way is part of the point, since the case for the architecture depends on the baseline genuinely struggling. Three published methods are also compared: a Fourier-only PINN with a single global scale, testing whether fixing spectral bias alone suffices; an XPINN with soft enforcement and no embedding, testing whether decomposition alone suffices; and a smoothed-interface PINN following Nohra and Dufour, testing the opposite interface choice. FDTD appears in timing comparisons only, as the reference rather than an accuracy competitor.

The architecture makes three changes to XPINN: per-subdomain Fourier embeddings (F), the corrected interface treatment (D), and adaptive sampling (A). The ablation removes each in turn, testing five configurations: baseline with none, F only, D only, F and D together, and the full architecture. Everything else is held fixed, including geometry, reference solution, network size, optimizer schedule, and training length, and each configuration runs three times with different random seeds, reported as mean and spread, since single-run PINN results are noisy enough that one number can reflect the initialization rather than the architecture.

In the overall study, the independent variable is which components are active, and the dependent variables are the metrics above, with global and interface-region relative L2 error as the main outcomes and inference time as secondary. The control is the standard PINN and the experimental condition is the full architecture, with the three published methods between them to show whether the combination beats its individual parts, the real claim since none of the three is new alone. Confounders are controlled where possible: random seeds and sampling vary, handled by three seeds and reported spread; hardware affects timing, so timing runs on one machine; and penalty weights and training budget are held constant so no configuration benefits from different weighting or longer training. Two simplifications are acknowledged rather than controlled, the perfect-conductor treatment of copper and the fixed-property model of FR-4, since both simplify the reference and the model equally and so do not bias the comparison, though they limit how directly the absolute error figures carry to a physical PCB.

sections.heading: References
paragraphs: [1] Raissi, M., Perdikaris, P., & Karniadakis, G.E. (2019). Physics-informed neural networks: A deep learning framework for solving forward and inverse problems involving nonlinear partial differential equations. Journal of Computational Physics, 378, 686-707.

[2] Jagtap, A.D., & Karniadakis, G.E. (2020). Extended physics-informed neural networks (XPINNs): A generalized space-time domain decomposition based deep learning framework for nonlinear partial differential equations. Communications in Computational Physics, 28(5), 2002-2041.

[3] Tancik, M., Srinivasan, P., Mildenhall, B., et al. (2020). Fourier features let networks learn high frequency functions in low dimensional domains. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 33, 7537-7547.

[4] Wang, S., Wang, H., & Perdikaris, P. (2021). On the eigenvector bias of Fourier feature networks: From regression to solving multi-scale PDEs with physics-informed neural networks. Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering, 384, 113938.
[5] Nohra, M., & Dufour, S. (2024). Physics-informed neural networks for the numerical modeling of steady-state and transient electromagnetic problems with discontinuous media. arXiv:2406.04380.
[6] Nohra, M., & Dufour, S. (2024). Approximating electromagnetic fields in discontinuous media using a single physics-informed neural network. arXiv:2407.20833.
[7] Oskooi, A.F., Roundy, D., Ibanescu, M., et al. (2010). MEEP: A flexible free-software package for electromagnetic simulations by the FDTD method. Computer Physics Communications, 181(3), 687-702.
[8] Lu, L., Meng, X., Mao, Z., & Karniadakis, G.E. (2021). DeepXDE: A deep learning library for solving differential equations. SIAM Review, 63(1), 208-228.

[9] Wu, C., Zhu, M., Tan, Q., Kartha, Y., & Lu, L. (2023). A comprehensive study of non-adaptive and residual-based adaptive sampling for physics-informed neural networks. Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering, 403, 115671.
